name: Liquid facelift

lead: A liquid facelift uses injectable fillers, usually hyaluronic acid, in several facial areas in one session to restore volume and contour without surgery. The change is visible immediately, giving a lifted, more youthful face.

Fillers replace volume lost with aging in facial compartments. Most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months. The phrase is a marketing term, also used in a 2018 case series for a water-jet liposuction technique alongside surgical facelift; the literature is mostly narrative reviews.

paras: A clinician plans several injection areas, such as cheeks, temples, jawline and lines around the mouth, and places filler in one session. People repeat it as the filler gradually breaks down.
Common effects are bruising, redness and pain. Rare but serious risks include infection, lumps, vascular embolization and permanent vision loss. Fillers are FDA-regulated medical devices.

angle.text: A liquid facelift is the marketing term for placing fillers, often hyaluronic acid, in several face areas in one session to restore volume and contour without surgery. The lifted look is visible immediately and lasts around six months for most fillers.

lead: 'Liquid facelift' is a marketing term for non-surgical facial rejuvenation that uses injectable fillers, often hyaluronic acid, to restore volume and contour in several areas of the face in one session. People use it to lift the look of hollow cheeks, soft jawlines and folds without an operation, with shorter recovery than surgery. [1][2][3] The term is also used in one 2018 case series for a different technique: water jet-assisted liposuction used alongside surgical rhytidectomy. [4]

Injectable fillers are classified by the US FDA as medical devices, and Wikipedia reports that most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months, with exercise and manual labour able to shorten duration. It lists bruising, lumps, infection and, rarely, vision loss from vascular embolisation among risks.[5]

Related non-surgical lifting approaches described in the literature include radiofrequency tightening, PDO thread lifts combined with fillers, and surgical volume replacement at the time of a facelift. [2][6][7][8]

A 2010 Missouri Medicine review concluded that in patients with mild jowling a nonsurgical liquid facelift can approach the results of surgical facelifting, while patients with significant jowling are better served by adding volume replacement during a rhytidectomy.[2]

paras: A 2010 article in Missouri Medicine describes a blending of surgical and nonsurgical techniques driven by patients' desire for an un-operated look and shorter recovery, and discusses volume loss in the facial skeleton and soft-tissue compartments, contrasting autologous fat grafting and injectable fillers with surgical rhytidectomy. [2] A 2009 nurse-practitioner article and a 2024 oral and maxillofacial surgery atlas chapter are titled 'The liquid facelift' and 'Liquid Facelift'. [3][1]

The Missouri Medicine review says that in patients with mild jowling the liquid facelift can approach the results seen in surgical face-lifting, while in patients with significant jowling, adding volume replacement at the time of rhytidectomy enhances rejuvenation and may allow less aggressive surgical dissection. [2] The same review discusses anatomical change in the facial skeleton and soft-tissue compartments as the rationale for replacing volume rather than only pulling skin. [2]
Typical target areas named in the filler literature include the cheeks and mid-face, the jawline and the lips, with fillers also used for fine lines and folds.[5]

The facial skeleton and soft-tissue compartments change with age, with bone resorption and fat loss contributing to hollowing, folds and jowls. The liquid facelift approach replaces lost volume in several places in the same session, as opposed to only pulling skin tight as in a traditional rhytidectomy.[2] Patients choose it for an un-operated look, less downtime and the option of repeat treatment.[2]

The same literature compares volume-restoring options such as autologous fat grafting and injectable fillers with procedures like subperiosteal midface lifting and facelift surgery, and describes a blending of surgical and nonsurgical techniques.[2]

Hyaluronic acid is the most common filler material; others include collagen, poly(lactic acid), polyethylene glycol and poly(methyl methacrylate). Crosslinking improves durability, and PLLA works by stimulating collagen production as it degrades rather than by giving immediate volume. [5]

Fillers are used to correct wrinkles and folds, restore volume lost with age, and enhance the lips, cheeks and jawline. Superficial and mid-dermal placement is used for fine lines and firmer fillers go deeper for severe wrinkles. Results depend on skin health, provider skill and filler type, and exercise can shorten duration by increasing blood flow. [5]

Combination approaches appear in case literature: a 2022 case report described a 39-year-old man treated in two sessions with PDO cog threads followed by hyaluronic acid filler, and reported improved sagging within a week and high satisfaction. [7] A 2003 clinical trial treated 20 areas in 17 patients with a radiofrequency device to the brow and jowls and reported gradual tightening in most patients with no adverse effects. [6]

Case series: a 2018 series of 25 patients (median age 56) in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery described facial water jet-assisted liposuction for contouring, fat harvesting and hydrodissection of the skin flap in surgical facelifts, under the heading 'liquid facelift'. Reported discomfort, bleeding, swelling and haematoma scores were low, there was no skin necrosis or revision surgery, and 13 patients completing a FACE-Q survey reported high satisfaction. The sample was small and retrospective.[4]

Review: the Missouri Medicine review described above is a narrative comparison of volume replacement and surgery; it reports that for mild jowling the liquid facelift can approach surgical results.[2] No randomised controlled trial of the filler-based liquid facelift was identified.

Related non-surgical lifting: a 2003 clinical trial in 17 patients (20 areas) of a radiofrequency device to the brow and jowls reported gradual tightening in most patients with no adverse effects.[6] A 2022 case report described a 39-year-old man treated with PDO cog threads and then hyaluronic acid filler, with improved sagging within a week and high satisfaction.[7] A 2026 meta-analysis of 26 studies (2,827 patients) on thread lifting found pooled incidences of swelling 34%, bruising 26%, visible or palpable threads 10%, and skin dimpling 7%, with substantial heterogeneity. It described thread lifting as generally safe but with variable complication rates.[8]

Wikipedia reports that common filler effects include bruising, redness, pain and itching, less commonly infection and allergic reactions causing lumps or scarring, and rarely permanent vision loss or delayed skin necrosis from embolization. In the US only a small number of fillers are approved; in the UK and EU a CE mark certifies production standards without requiring proof of efficacy. Who may inject fillers is debated between physicians and other licensed injectors. [5]

Fillers are not neurotoxins like botulinum toxin. The US FDA has approved only a small number as medical devices, and in the UK and EEA fillers are non-prescription medical devices carrying a CE mark, with over 140 on the market. [5]

Missouri Medicine attributes the technique to patient demand for an un-operated look and shorter recovery, which has led to a blending of surgical and nonsurgical methods. [2] Because 'liquid facelift' is a marketing label rather than a defined procedure, what it includes varies between clinics, and the literature uses it for both filler treatment and a surgical adjunct. [1][4]
